lede: A pregnancy needs a chain of events, and every method of contraception breaks one link. Work out which link, and you can explain any method — including the ones you have not been taught.
can: Explain how a condom, the pill, an implant and sterilisation each prevent pregnancy.
Sort a method into CCEA's three groups: mechanical, chemical and surgical.
Describe in vitro fertilisation and weigh up its advantages and disadvantages.

md: A pregnancy needs a chain of events, and every link has to hold. Contraception works by breaking one of them. Fertility treatment works by doing one of them somewhere else. Once you can see the chain, you can explain a method you were never taught.

md:
**The pill and the implant** change hormone levels, so **no ovum develops** — link 1 never happens.
**Male sterilisation** cuts the **sperm tubes**, so sperm cannot leave.
**The condom** is a **barrier**, so sperm never reach the ovum.
**Female sterilisation** cuts the **oviducts**, so the ovum and the sperm cannot meet.

Name the link and you have the mechanism. That is what the marks are for.

options: it changes hormone levels, so no ovum develops
it is a barrier that stops sperm reaching the ovum
answer: it changes hormone levels, so no ovum develops
explain: It changes hormone levels so no ovum develops or is released. Calling it a barrier is the answer for a condom, and it is the commonest wrong turn on this question.

title: Why the grouping matters more than it looks
md:
CCEA sorts contraception into **mechanical**, **chemical** and **surgical**. Almost every revision site sorts it into *hormonal* and *non-hormonal* instead, because that is how the other boards teach it.

The two groupings cut across each other: a condom and sterilisation are both *non-hormonal*, and CCEA calls one **mechanical** and the other **surgical**. Use CCEA's three words on the answer line.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Contraception"
why: A quick second pass over the methods, now that you have the chain to hang them on. It is made for another board, so it sorts them into hormonal and non-hormonal — translate each one back into CCEA's three groups as you watch, and the question underneath asks you to do exactly that.

title: Two things to let pass in that clip
md: Clips made for the other boards name methods CCEA does not — **coils**, **patches**, **injections**, **diaphragms**, **spermicides** — and they usually give the pill's mechanism as **inhibiting FSH**. FSH is not on this specification at all, and the wording CCEA marks is **changes hormone levels**. Keep to the four methods and the three groups above.

prompt: CCEA sorts contraception into three groups. A condom belongs to the ______ group.
explain: Mechanical, because it works as a physical barrier. The pill and the implant are chemical; sterilisation is surgical.

text: 3. The one thing only a barrier can do

alt: A microscope image of a human ovum held steady by a blunt glass pipette on the left while a fine needle on the right pierces it to deliver a single sperm.
credit: Dr Elena Kontogianni, Wikimedia Commons, CC0
caption: Fertilisation in a dish, under a microscope. In this clinic one sperm is being injected into the ovum; CCEA asks only that the ova and sperm are mixed in a dish.
prompt: Which step of in vitro fertilisation is this, and where is it happening?

md:
A condom stops something **passing between two people**. So it is the only method here that also prevents the spread of **sexually transmitted infections** — **HIV**, which leads to AIDS, and **chlamydia**, which can cause **infertility** if it is left untreated.

The pill changes what happens inside **one** body, so it cannot do that. If a question asks for an advantage of a condom over the pill, this is the answer it wants.

prompt: Which advantage does a condom have that the contraceptive pill does not?
options: it helps to prevent sexually transmitted infections
it is more reliable at preventing pregnancy
answer: it helps to prevent sexually transmitted infections
explain: Only a barrier stops an infection passing between partners. On the survey data the pill is in fact the more reliable of the two at preventing pregnancy.

title: Worked example: 'Explain how taking the contraceptive pill stops a pregnancy starting. [2]'
md:
**Step 1 — find the link it breaks.** The pill acts on link 1, before an ovum has developed. Locating the cut stops you writing a barrier answer.
**Step 2 — first half.** It **changes hormone levels**. **[1]**
**Step 3 — second half.** So **no ovum develops or is released**. **[1]**
**Step 4 — check.** Nothing about blocking or killing sperm.

A mechanism answer always needs the cause **and** the consequence.

prompt: In the survey shown, 70 of 1000 women using the contraceptive pill became pregnant in a year. What percentage is that?
explain: 70 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 7.0%. Most of those failures are missed doses rather than the drug failing.

md:
Causes of infertility include a **lack of sperm**, sperm **without flagella**, **blocked oviducts**, a **lack of ova** and a **lack of the right hormones**.

Treatment, in the specification's own words: **hormones to produce multiple ova**, **in vitro fertilisation**, and the **transfer of several embryos into the uterus**.

Say *in a dish* for where the fertilisation happens. "In a laboratory" has not been enough.

prompt: Why is a woman given hormones at the start of in vitro fertilisation?
options: so that several ova ripen at once
to make the sperm swim faster
to fertilise the ova in the dish
answer: so that several ova ripen at once
explain: To produce multiple ova. A normal cycle releases one; the treatment needs several, because most will not go on to a pregnancy.

text: 6. Deciding, and the reasons science cannot settle

md:
Treatment is not a guarantee: in this clinic's year, 32.0% of cycles started by women under 35 ended in a live birth, falling to 11.0% for women of 40 to 42. It is also physically and emotionally hard, and transferring several embryos can lead to a multiple birth.

Contraception and fertility treatment both **raise ethical issues for some people**. Those are questions science alone cannot answer, and an exam asking for an *ethical* reason wants a religious or moral one — not cost, and not side effects.

prompt: A question asks for an ethical reason why someone might choose not to use contraception. Which answer earns the mark?
options: their religious beliefs teach that it is wrong
answer: their religious beliefs teach that it is wrong
explain: An ethical reason is about right and wrong. Cost and side effects are practical reasons, and examiners report that candidates often give those instead.

md:
Explain how the **condom**, the **pill**, an **implant** and **sterilisation** each prevent pregnancy, by naming the link each one breaks.
Sort any of them into CCEA's three groups: **mechanical**, **chemical**, **surgical**.
Say that only the condom also prevents **HIV** and **chlamydia** passing between partners, and which tube is cut in male and in female sterilisation.
Describe **in vitro fertilisation** and give causes of infertility *(Higher Tier)*.
Give an **advantage and a disadvantage** with reasons, and tell an ethical reason from a practical one.

Contraception comes as two or three one-mark parts inside a bigger reproduction question. The first mark is usually a method named or identified; the last is an ethical reason or a disadvantage. Stuck on a mechanism? Name the **link** it breaks and then say **so…** — the cause on its own is half an answer. Give CCEA's group word too: mechanical, chemical or surgical.
